dropped.reason: The only relocation count anywhere in this project's documents exists solely as something Bank staff told the Bank's evaluators. The Evaluation Group's review of 3 June 2021 says: "The project team provided following information on land acquisition: the actual resettlement impacts included 650 mu (43 ha) of permanent land acquisition with impact on 478 farmers' and 370 workers' livelihood, and relocation of 167 households with 395 persons, among which 51 households moved into their replacement apartments and 116 households got cash compensation." The same review says plainly, in the sentence above it, "The ICR does not discuss the magnitude of land acquisition." Checked in the outcome document: the completion report of 9 December 2020, paragraph 80, is the project's only account of what happened, and it gives no relocation figure at all - "According to the final external resettlement monitoring report for the project, there were 1,249 project affected persons due to construction of the transfer stations, the KWTF, the Ningbo municipal waste disposal center and Reconstruction of Dongqiao Town Xuanpei Village" - and then records that "as of the time of this ICR, all land acquisition and resettlement related compensatory activities have been completed in full". Paragraph 82 says complaints received were recorded and addressed properly. A count of people affected is not a count of people moved, and the review's own account of the outside monitor's June 2020 report is that the resettlement was fully completed, incomes and housing fully restored, with no pending issue or complaint. The 683 persons, 5,360 square metres of houses and 55,300 square metres of business buildings that the review prints are the 2012 resettlement plan's figures in the future tense, attributed by the review itself to the appraisal document. The review also states that Dongqiao Town was demolished for the kitchen waste facility and had to be rebuilt at a new site, but attributes that too to the project team's clarification rather than to a document. Neither limb of the forward rule is met on any document.

No outcome document counts anyone relocated, and both outcome documents record the opposite of harm. Checked in the outcome documents: the completion report of 24 June 2012 says "Land acquisition and resettlement for all investment projects have been satisfactorily implemented. All compensation have been paid to the affected people based on the Resettlement Action Plan (RAP), all relocated households have completed the construction of replacement houses, and all proposed rehabilitation measures indicated in the RAP have been implemented for the affected villages. Income and livelihood of the affected people have been restored and even increased compared with that before resettlement." It gives no count with that sentence. The two problems it names are a change of site for the Rudong biomass plant, resolved by the owners leasing rather than selling the fuel storage land, and a revised land acquisition estimate for access roads in Inner Mongolia, resolved by an updated plan approved by the Bank. The field-based Project Performance Assessment Report of 30 June 2017, paragraph 3.21, says "The project encountered no significant issues with land acquisition and resettlement for the pilot-investment subprojects" and that the Inner Mongolia issues were satisfactorily addressed during supervision. ICIJ's 570 traces to the appraisal document and the 2004 resettlement plans, which count 31 households with 147 people affected at the Pingtan wind farm, "with none needing relocation", and 25 households with 103 people at the Rudong plant site. Those are plan figures in the future tense for impacts the two outcome documents say caused no issue. Neither limb of the forward rule is met.

This row is the second IBRD loan of the same programme as P067828, not a Global Environment Facility grant; the assessment report describes it as "a second IBRD loan (P096158) to finance two additional pilot investments". The completion report of 24 June 2012 covers both loans and the GEF grant together, so the two rows share outcome documents. Checked in the outcome documents: the completion report of 24 June 2012 and the field-based Project Performance Assessment Report of 30 June 2017, both of which cover this number, count nobody relocated and record no harm, saying compensation was fully paid, replacement houses completed, incomes restored or increased, and no significant land acquisition or resettlement issues. ICIJ's 131 traces to the resettlement action plan for the Huitengxile wind farm and the resettlement policy framework, both plans. Neither limb of the forward rule is met.

ICIJ's 702 is a resettlement plan's affected-population count for a heat supply pipeline, and no outcome document carries it or anything like it. The October 2007 plan for the Shandong Huangtai power plant heat supply pipe network says "the actually affected population is 225 households with 702 persons (in which 146 households with 462 persons are affected by land acquisition, 53 households with 163 persons are affected by relocation and 26 households with 77 persons are affected by both land requisition and relocation)" - a survey of expected impacts, in a plan. Checked in the outcome documents: the completion report of 25 February 2015, paragraph 46, is the project's only account of social safeguards and it is about workers, not land: "The implementation of involuntary resettlement was rated satisfactory as the approved Resettlement Plan Framework and resettlement plans associated with the nine closed small power plants had been followed... Adequate compensation and social protection measures for settlement of affected workers were provided. The post evaluation activity did not identify any remaining social issues." The Evaluation Group's review of 9 June 2015 repeats this. The field-based Project Performance Assessment Report of 13 June 2018, paragraph 2.14, says "This ensured that most workers did not need to relocate as there were similar opportunities nearby", and its summary of what did not work says the team had underestimated the government's commitment to compensatory measures, so the funds set aside to facilitate the closures were not needed. No outcome document counts anyone relocated or records a loss. Neither limb of the forward rule is met.

No outcome document counts anyone relocated, and the only grievance either records is about road signage. Checked in the outcome documents: the completion report of 27 March 2018, paragraph 64, says "Project implementation was in line with the social safeguards frameworks and plans, and there were no reports of major social safeguards issues in the progress reports (only minor issues about traffic control during construction, which were addressed by the contractors and project manager)". Its borrower section, item A.1.c, says "All resettlements on NR1B and NR6A were fully paid by GoL in accordance with Law and Regulations prior to the start of constructions." Its mission record says "The RAP implementation has been completed with compensation and required support provided to all Project Affected Households (PAH)... The PAHs met confirmed the receipt of cash compensation from the Project", and that the grievances raised were "mainly related to the need for further improvement of road safety measures such as traffic control sign posts at some points of the NR6A". ICIJ's 399 traces to the 2008 and 2009 resettlement plans and ethnic group development plans for roads 1B and 6A, which project 24 households to be relocated, 1,109 square metres of structures to be demolished and 26 households affected, all in the future tense. The candidate sentences flagged as deaths in the pre-extracted brief are road-safety indicators and a plan's list of future risks, not deaths. One conflict is left unreconciled: the Evaluation Group's review of 24 May 2018 says "The ICR author advised there were no persons affected by the project", while the completion report itself describes compensation paid to project-affected households on both roads. Neither limb of the forward rule is met on any document.

No outcome document counts anyone relocated or records a loss. Checked in the outcome documents: the completion report of 24 February 2017, paragraph 49, says the involuntary resettlement policy was triggered because the project built preventive health centres where no health facility had stood before, that "The activities implemented, including the assessment of socioeconomic impacts, reimbursement of losses, and recovery of income, were carefully prepared and fully implemented", and that the mid-term review report "confirmed the construction of 30 DPHCs with no complaints on compensation/resettlement". The Evaluation Group's review of 23 June 2017 repeats this and finds full compliance with the safeguard policies. ICIJ's 366 traces to the November 2009 resettlement policy framework, which says "There are 98 housholds impacted by the project. However, no residential land will be acquired" and lists land to be taken by district, mostly public vacant land. That framework also carries a null sentence - "acquisition of any private land for construction of district care centers will not be necessary and OP 4.12 on Involuntary Resettlement will not be triggered by any component under the project" - which is noted here as evidence and is not what decided this drop; the two outcome documents are. Neither limb of the forward rule is met.

The compensation delay this project records has its consequence named in the same paragraph, and the consequence is to the works. Checked in the outcome documents: the completion report of 12 December 2013, section 2.4, says "Land acquisition was carried out following the provision stipulated in the RAPs and the RPF. The project complied with social safeguard policies. However, the project experienced substantial delays in the implementation of site clearances and compensation... These delays had considerable adverse impact on the progress of civil works, particularly for subprojects in Hanoi, Thai Nguyen, Bac Ninh and Ha Tinh." Section 2.1 gives three causes of the delay: late mobilisation of government counterpart funding for compensation, disagreement between district committees and affected persons over the amount of compensation, and weak collaboration between the provincial project management units and the district committees. The Evaluation Group's review of 12 December 2015 repeats the same sentences and the same stated consequence. Neither document counts a household, names a site, says any compensation went unpaid or below replacement cost, or says any livelihood was not restored. The harm named is to the progress of the civil works. ICIJ's 360 traces to the November 2008 resettlement plan, which counts 79 households affected by agricultural land acquisition in four sub-projects in Hai Duong province, and to the appraisal document of 22 November 2004, which says "No household will be relocated and assets affected are mainly agricultural land, trees and crops." Neither limb of the forward rule is met.

The component that would have displaced people was never carried out, and the completion report says so in terms. Checked in the outcome document: the completion report of 18 May 2012, section 2.4, says "Since the restoration of the mudflats in Plots A3 and A5 did not take place, those engaged in aquaculture were not displaced and their livelihoods were not affected by the project. Therefore, there was no need to implement the RAP as envisaged. Consultation activities envisaged in the RAP were, however, carried out and fishermen were offered compensation on a voluntary basis. Forty-eight fishmen, including 10 women have been employed at the Wetlands Center as wage laborers. Nevertheless, this compensation scheme has not had any impact on reducing fishing activity in the area." Section 2.2 says the inter-tidal mudflats were not restored, that fish harvesting in the area in fact increased and the number of fishermen rose significantly since appraisal, and that "A resettlement action plan was prepared early in the project to identify those harvesting fishery resources from the project area along with measures for restoring their livelihoods, but it was not carried out." ICIJ's 348 traces to the April 2006 resettlement plan, which projects 114 households with 348 persons affected in Andong and Zhouxiang towns and 2,508.3 mu of aquaculture area affected - a plan for a component that did not happen. The project's shortfall here is a conservation measure not delivered, not a displacement. Neither limb of the forward rule is met.

No relocation count and no unmet loss, on the project's own documents. The Project Performance Assessment Report of 21 June 2011 is a joint report covering five projects in Tanzania and Uganda, and this project, Credit 3888-TA, is Annex B. Annex B's safeguards section, paragraph 18, says the project was category A, that full environmental and social assessments were done at preparation, and that "The Involuntary Resettlement Policy (OP 4.12) was triggered for Zanzibar because of land purchases and a resettlement framework and RAPs for roads were implemented based on procedures and guidelines outlined in the governing policies. All compensation claims and grievances were settled. Some 870 persons were affected at a cost of TZS 250 million." Annex B paragraph 19 covers the railway: a resettlement plan was prepared "since 145 project-affected people were identified living near the rail right-of-way who could be affected due to increased train speeds. Since the reverse happened, and train speeds fell due to the deteriorating condition of the railways, the risk did not materialize, and the RAP was never implemented." So nobody was moved for the railway either. Annex B also records, in its borrower performance section, that the railway operator was responsible for the environmental cleaning and for implementing the resettlement plan and that "There were delays in these activities due to the retrenchment of staff, but a consultant was employed to assist with completing the work"; no document says who was affected by that delay or for how long. The completion report of 29 June 2010 was read for the outcome and agrees: its paragraph 45 gives Table 1, counting 870 persons affected on three Zanzibar road sections, 174 on residential houses and 696 on commercial properties, and Table 2 showing actual compensation of TZS 250.20 million paid, under the sentence "All compensation claims and grievances were settled accordingly based on the monitoring and evaluation plan." Its paragraph 46 gives the same account of the unimplemented railway plan. What remains is a count of people affected with compensation paid in full and no count of anyone relocated, which the forward rule treats as a drop. Two candidate sentences offered for this row came from the wrong half of the joint assessment report and are not evidence about this project: "For those components that were completed there was no relocation of households" and "About 1,000 people were displaced and a further 25,000 adversely affected by the severe floods" both sit in Annex A, which evaluates Tanzania's Second Integrated Roads Project, Credit 2598-TA, and its El Nino flood rehabilitation component. Neither was used.

The resettlement in this project's area was paid for by another lender and the credit financed none of it. The completion report of 30 December 2014 says in its footnote 1: "Involuntary resettlement within the targeted TFCAs was not an objective of the TFCATDP, and no project funding was allocated to resettlement activities. However, the World Bank agreed to provide advisory services to involuntary resettlement activities funded by the KfW in Limpopo National Park, but outside of TFCATDP implementation and Bank supervision." The same footnote says the implementation of both resettlement plans "faced some issues", blaming the government's lack of knowledge and commitment, KfW's lack of knowledge of resettlement safeguards and insufficient budget, and the Bank's lack of a local social scientist. The outcome document was read for a relocation count and holds none. Its Table 10, which looks like one, is the opposite: the number of families living inside three parks fell from 2,050 to 448, and paragraph 38 explains that this was done by moving the park boundaries, "excising (i.e. re-demarcation) the more densely populated areas so that fewer people would have to be resettled". The evaluation review of 23 November 2015 adds nothing on resettlement beyond naming the policy. ICIJ's 691 for this row is the figure in the April 2008 resettlement plan for Macavene village, which states that "the population of Macavene is 691 people in 128 household units" and plans to move those 128 households to Banga and Tihovene; it is a plan census, not an outcome. A Mail and Guardian report of 6 April 2018 describes about 2,000 families resettled from eight villages in the Massingir area, with no farming land, no jobs and water now bought rather than drawn, but names no funder, so it cannot be tied to this credit.

A count of affected people with compensation paid, and no relocation. The completion report of 25 February 2022 says at paragraph 64 that for the transmission main between Corumana and Machava "The RAP was successfully implemented, as the 387 affected people were adequately compensated, and the 93 claims received were properly addressed." The outcome document's own Annex 5 was also read: its paragraph 6 says a full resettlement plan was prepared and implemented for the 94 km of transmission main from Corumana Dam to the Machava Distribution Centre and that "A total of 393 PAPs were identified and adequately compensated" — 393 against the 387 in paragraph 64, unreconciled in the same report. Annex 5 paragraph 7 says the post-resettlement evaluation found that affected people received appropriate compensation and were able to restore their livelihoods where applicable, and paragraph 3 says no severe or permanently disabling health and safety incident was reported on any contract and no deaths. The route was densely populated, mostly street vendors and public utilities, and the report says all grievances and complaints were adequately and timely resolved. No document counts anyone relocated and none records an unpaid or short payment.

No documented loss to identifiable people. The completion report of 27 March 2014 was read for the outcome. Its resettlement bullet says the plan's provisions were invoked only for the 66 kV line from Nairobi North Substation to Westlands, that from August 2011 the utility "paid compensation to 113 eligible owners of structures/houses along the right of way for this transmission line, in accordance with the RAP", and that the affected people who lost land, crops, trees, structures or dwellings "were satisfied with the RAP implementation and payments", witnessed by the chief of the Karura location whose office verified ownership and kept the census list. The one disputed strand is the Lavington substation in Nairobi, and it did not turn on a recorded loss. The Inspection Panel's own case page for case 79 records a Request received 10 May 2012 from Mr Peter Usher on behalf of the Njumbi Road Residents' Association, alleging the substation development was "illegal, inappropriate, environmentally unsound and poses a danger to people living near the development" — an anticipated danger. The Panel registered the Request on 24 May 2012 and did not recommend an investigation, publishing its eligibility report on 25 July 2012 and saying the legitimacy of the siting process was outside its purview and before the National Environment Tribunal. The completion report records the Tribunal's ruling of 1 March 2013 cancelling the environmental licence of 24 February 2011 and revoking the approval of 30 December 2010, and directing the utility to relocate the substation; the utility appealed to the High Court on 2 April 2013 and the substation was left incomplete. No document records a death, injury, arrest, unpaid compensation or lost livelihood. The completion report's monitoring table also carries a row for "Evictions of Maasai communities in the Lake Navaisha area", and its own entry states the evictions "are related neither to KenGen nor to the Olkaria II project", with no count and no date, so nothing can be built on it.

The harm the outcome document records is real but names nobody and nowhere. The completion report of 29 June 2018 says at paragraph 83 that "The project complied with all applicable environmental and social safeguards", and then: "However, in some project locations, there were delays due to lack of capacity for undertaking necessary assessments and using necessary tools; delays related to compensation and resettlement for project-affected people (PAPs); lack of sufficient attention and compensation for livelihoods-related losses; lack of safeguards experts in secondary cities (early in the project); poor documentation for safeguards in some cities; and late implementation of grievance redress systems that were recommended to be strengthened with limited progress." It does not say which of the cities — Addis Ababa, Gondar, Hawassa, Jimma, Mekelle and Dire Dawa — nor how many people, nor what the livelihood losses were. The only count in the outcome document is paragraph 84: "A total of 89 project affected persons were compensated, following the RAPs." The resettlement plan of October 2014 for the Kaliti wastewater treatment plant and sewer lines in Addis Ababa plans for 269 affected households, of which "31 households will lose their residential housing units resulting in relocation" and 238 would lose part of a housing unit, a fence or similar; those are plan figures and no outcome document carries them or any other relocation count. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 30 September 2018 drops the shortcomings altogether and says only that "All 89 project affected people were compensated following the RAPs". This is the closest call in the batch: the completion report does record compensation delays and under-compensated livelihood losses, which is limb (b) language, but with no place, no count and no identifiable people it cannot be written as a card without inventing the missing parts.

Land taken, compensation paid in full before the works, and no relocation. The completion report of 25 June 2015 was read for the outcome. Its paragraph 50 says involuntary resettlement was triggered because upgrading the B6 Belle Rive to Quartier Militaire road required land acquisition and compensation, that an abbreviated resettlement plan — called a Land Acquisition Plan in Mauritius — was prepared, disclosed before appraisal and "implemented in a manner satisfactory to the Bank before the commencement of respective works", under almost bi-monthly supervision, and that "The compensation for the land acquisition was paid by the GoM's own resources in the amount of US$1.1 million", held in a separate escrow account at the Ministry of Housing and Lands. The report's paragraph 40 records that the mid-term review of February 2013 found "the progress of compensation for the land acquisition for the B6 works was slow and posed a risk that the compensation process would not be completed before completion of the upgrading of the road", and states that all the review's issues "were addressed and resolved by the project closing". No document counts affected people or households, none counts anyone relocated, and none records a payment unmade or below replacement cost.

The lender's own outcome documents say the works that took the land were not financed by the project, and the project's own land take exists only as a plan. The completion report of 3 December 2015, paragraph 33, says: "During the course of project implementation, the need for land acquisition arose at passing loops and near Yenice Logistic Village (which was not financed by the Bank but adjacent to the project)." The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 30 June 2016 repeats that clause and cites it to page 9 of the completion report, so it is the report's statement and not a separate finding. The appraisal document of 12 May 2005 did not trigger the involuntary resettlement policy and says "no resettlement or land acquisition is involved". The actual, past harm in the file is the urgent expropriation at Yenice: the resettlement plan of March 2011 records that TCDD's executive board decided on 25 January 2008 to expropriate about 277,249.71 square metres at the Yenice terminal for a logistics village, that a Council of Ministers decree of 31 March 2008 authorised urgent expropriation under Article 27, that the Tarsus courts set the value of 155 parcels at TRY 17,977,032.97, that TCDD valued 47 private parcels covering 220,553.71 square metres at TRY 5,620,188.46, that four owners settled at the June 2010 meeting, that TRY 5,308,128.58 set by the courts was remitted on 30 June 2010 into accounts opened in the parcel owners' names before the courts granted entry, and that valuation lawsuits were filed on 14 July 2010 for the 43 parcels where no agreement was reached. All of that predates the 2011 restructuring by which the Bank first brought Yenice inside a resettlement plan, and none of it is on works the loan financed. The land take for the project's own works is plan-level only: 74 parcels totalling 302,388.16 square metres at an estimated TRY 9.2 million, 41 households losing land, three households whose houses would be affected. Checked in the outcome documents: paragraphs 16 and 33 of the completion report, its results framework, and the safeguards section of the review. Neither records any land acquired, any household paid, or how the 43 court cases ended, and no Turkish court record or news report of the Yenice expropriations was found. The drop turns on the lender-link test and not on the forward rule; if a document is ever found tying the loan to the Yenice land take, or recording how the 43 valuation suits ended, the row is worth reopening. ICIJ's estimate for this project is 256.

The outcome document's whole quantitative content is a count of people affected, and it records that nobody moved and everybody was paid. The completion report of 30 October 2013, in its involuntary resettlement section, says KEGOC "acquired about 14 hectares of land for permanent use and 555 hectares for temporary use", that "in total, 316 persons (land users) have been affected. None had to be resettled, and all received reasonable cash compensation", and that "all compensation has been completed prior to loan closure". The finding it does make is procedural: "construction of the line started prior to the Bank's formal approval of a Land Acquisition Plan", after which a plan was approved with "relevant retroactive measures" to bring compensation into line with the resettlement policy. ICIJ's 316 is that affected count. That leaves neither limb of the forward rule: no relocation, and no loss recorded to any identified person. This is the same shape as four rows dropped in this batch, including Talimarjan and Kakheti, where land was taken, everyone was paid and no complaint was recorded. Checked in the outcome documents: the safeguards section and the Bank-performance section of the completion report, and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 27 June 2014. One route back is the Land Acquisition Plan itself, which carries no date on its cover and gives its figures as of May 2012: its Table 2.2 breaks the 316 into 222 land users in Enbekshikazakh, 58 in Ili, 20 in Raimbek, 13 in Talgar and 3 in Kapshagai town, with a footnote that "compensation payment agreements are under conclusion", and its Appendix 2 lists each land user by name with the area taken, the compensation amount and dates in 2011 and 2012. If those date columns can be read cleanly they may show land taken months before agreement for named people, which would be a documented harm; in the harvested text the table's columns are mangled and no such claim can be made from it. ICIJ's estimate for this project is 316.

The outcome document records no land taken and nobody moved. The completion report of 27 June 2015, paragraph 2.4.7, states: "There was no land acquisition under either the parent project or AFs, and there were no project affected people (PAPs) under the parent project and AF1. The total compensation of about KGS 350,000 (US$7,000) was paid to seven project affected businesses under AF2." Those seven are road-side businesses at the Nookat pass, compensated for profit lost during construction; the borrower's own section of the same report confirms the government issued a decree in March 2013 to release the money and that the plan was translated into Kyrgyz and presented to the seven. Neither limb of the forward rule is met: no relocation count, and no harm left standing after payment. Checked in the outcome document: paragraphs 2.4.4 to 2.4.8 on social safeguards, the results framework, and the borrower's completion contribution. The brief's harm hits were context, not project harm. Its two 'count with a relocation verb' sentences were the June 2010 civil unrest in Osh and Jalal-Abad, in which about 400,000 people were displaced, which the report gives as a reason for implementation delay, and the resettlement framework's recital of the policy threshold of 200 displaced people. Its 'arrests, police or force' sentence was a dispute between the Ministry of Transport and the Ministry of Internal Affairs over who owned the road safety strategy, and its death sentences were road fatality rate indicators. ICIJ's estimate for this project is 32.

The outcome document counts nine affected people in total and records each of them paid. The completion report of 26 May 2016, paragraph 38, says four resettlement action plans were prepared, for Bash-Karasuu, Naryn, Isfana and Tash-Kumyr, that "there were nine project affected people", and that only one complaint was received, addressed at the first grievance stage. Its borrower annex itemises the payments: five farmers in Orok ayil aymak received KGS 240,000 between them; a Naryn resident received KGS 25,000 for the loss of a partially constructed house plus a land plot from the mayor's office; an Isfana farmer received KGS 28,820 and a land plot; two Tash-Kumyr residents were paid KGS 6,000 each for removed trees. Neither limb is met: nobody was relocated, and no compensation is recorded as unpaid or below replacement cost. Checked in the outcome document: the safeguards paragraphs, the grievance record and the borrower's social safeguards annex. The brief's 'compensation unpaid or late' hit was a June 2014 meeting with the Osh vice-mayor at which two Tash-Kumyr residents agreed a water main route through their orchards and were given an explanation about outstanding amounts; the relevant plan budgets 12,200 som for four years of apricot crop and saplings, and the completion report records the payment made. ICIJ's estimate for this project is 9.

No outcome document counts land taken, households affected, or compensation left unpaid, and the harm language in the documents has delay to the works as its stated consequence. The completion report of 30 July 2024 says the utility's financial constraints "contributed to the documented delays, including those related to land acquisition and RAP compensations", and the next sentences give the consequence: the transmission rehabilitation finished in 2020, four years after the original closing date. Its social safeguards section says compliance was rated Satisfactory at closing, that all compliance reports found the abbreviated resettlement plans complied with the framework and national law, and that "most of the affected households (on average from 80 to 95 percent) were satisfied" with valuation, the size of compensation and the payment process. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 15 January 2025 repeats the 80 to 95 per cent. Neither limb is met. Checked in the outcome document: the social safeguards section, the factors affecting implementation, and the grievance record, which gives a garbled count of 157 grievances received and addressed. The resettlement policy framework of July 2015 says only that "it is expected that the number of persons to be relocated is minimal", a plan sentence with no outcome behind it. The brief's four harm hits were all recitals in the framework: the rule allowing possession before payment where compensation is pledged in court, the definition of replacement cost, the court deposit procedure, and the audit clause about livelihood restoration. ICIJ's estimate for this project is 440.

Two outcome documents agree that the land taken was smaller than planned and that every owner was paid without complaint. The Independent Evaluation Group's field-based Project Performance Assessment Report of 17 June 2020 says the road department "completed the land acquisition for the section between Vaziani and Gombori in 2010 and for the section between Gombori and Telavi in 2012", that design changes meant "the land acquisition involved 31 land plots instead of the 174 expected at appraisal", and that the department "fully compensated all landowners in accordance with the provisions of the resettlement action plan and received no complaints". The review of 10 June 2016 gives the same 31 against 174 and the same conclusion. Neither limb is met: no relocation, and no compensation recorded as unpaid or below replacement cost. Checked in the outcome documents: the social safeguards sections of both, and the assessment report's appendix B. A trap worth recording: the assessment report covers two projects, and the paragraph beginning "At appraisal, no land acquisition or resettlements were envisioned... Minor land acquisitions had to take place during project implementation" sits under the heading for the Secondary and Local Roads Project, P086277, not for this one. The brief's harm hits were road-safety fatality indicators and the entitlement matrix's recital of compensation at replacement cost. ICIJ's estimate for this project is 422.

The outcome document counts 118 affected people, mostly temporary, and records all of them paid. The completion report of 27 April 2015, paragraph 46, says the resettlement policy was triggered during implementation, that "118 Project Affected Persons (PAPs) in ten villages were identified", that they were "mainly affected by temporary restrictions to access or loss of trees and crops", and that "all PAPs were fully paid by the project closing date", with compensation of KGS 1,979,254, about US$50,000, paid exceptionally out of the credit itself. Neither limb is met. Checked in the outcome document: the safeguards section, the borrower's resettlement annex listing the ten villages, and the sections on the suspended sub-projects. One finding for another round rather than this row: the same report records that water schemes failed in 26 villages, and works were suspended before completion in Korumdu, Temir and Chelpek, under the predecessor Rural Water Supply and Sanitation Project, not under this one, "mostly associated with poor design of the water sources under the RWSSP", and that this project had to go back and fix them, deferring US$1.5 million of service work at Chelpek. The brief's harm hits were all framework recitals on eligibility and replacement cost. ICIJ's estimate for this project is 245.

The outcome document says the project avoided resettlement and gives no count of land taken or compensation unpaid. The completion report of 25 September 2020, paragraph 56, says the late appointment of the social safeguards specialist "caused delays in implementing the social safeguard instruments (for example, the RAP), which resulted in changing the locations of one of the wells as the implementation of the RAP was stalled", and that "the project avoided resettlement by changing the routes of some of the water and wastewater lines in some areas". The one specific complaint it records is about a contractor that delayed restoring a local road to its original condition after finishing works, raised directly to the Bank through a social network account; no people are identified and no count is given. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 25 June 2021 repeats the stalled plan and the avoided resettlement. Neither limb is met. Checked in the outcome document: paragraphs 55 and 56 on safeguards and the grievance record. The resettlement plan of January 2013 is plan-level only: 28 land owners along the new pipeline across four communes, with compensation estimated at 4,246,330 lek, about US$40,442, and a statement that no owner would be fully expropriated. ICIJ's estimate for this project is 137.

The outcome document records land taken from leasehold farms with compensation completed and no complaints. The completion report of 22 December 2016, paragraphs 50 to 52, says the project needed about 12.03 ha permanently and 159.42 ha temporarily from 114 leasehold farms in Kashkadarya and Samarkand, 90 in the first and 24 in the second; that "in total 141 farmers and Hokimiyats in eight districts... received compensation"; that land acquisition and compensation payments were "completed by April 2013"; that apart from 26.7 ha for the substation the takes averaged 1.1 ha; and that "to date, no complaints have been recorded". It explains the shifting counts, 114 in the plan, 147 in a supervision aide memoire, 141 in the final list, by a government farm-consolidation programme and by an audit that found six farmers had been paid in error and asked them to return the money, and says the entitlement matrix was never modified. Neither limb is met: nobody was relocated and no compensation is recorded as unpaid or below replacement cost. Checked in the outcome document: the involuntary resettlement paragraphs, the borrower's section, which says "land compensations have been paid during 2010-2013", and the social impact discussion. The brief's harm hits were monitoring-indicator headings in the resettlement plan of September 2010 that list "number of people not receiving compensation in time" as a thing to be measured, and a risk-matrix row in the appraisal document naming non-compliance as a risk to be managed. ICIJ's estimate for this project is 114.

Limb (a) is met on the face of it — the completion report of 27 June 2023 for the parent operation P111996 says the project "had to resettle 83 families living in precarious conditions inside the railroad right-of-way on the Deodoro and Belford Roxo lines", 70 rehoused and 13 taking cash — but the limit on limb (a) applies and no document records a loss on top of the move. The deciding sentence is in the state's own resettlement plan of September 2011, the document the card rested on, at section 1.4: "O reassentamento destas famílias é recomendado, pois as mesmas estão expostas ao risco de acidentes na ferrovia (descarrilhamento, atropelamento, etc.) ocupam a área, irregularmente, de forma precária e muito aquém do padrão mínimo de habitabilidade" — the resettlement is recommended because the families are exposed to the risk of rail accidents and are living below the minimum habitability standard. That makes this a hazard relocation on the plan's own words, which is the ground on which the map has dropped the Bogotá cases and on which this same batch drops corn-island-wetland-resettlement and rio-bogota-el-porvenir-resettlement. The evaluation review ICRR0023561 adds that "the project did not require the acquisition of any new land" and that the families "had been illegally occupying the right-of-way of an auxiliary rail line under SuperVia's concession". The completion report records the handling as satisfactory, in line with Bank guidelines, with no complaint, no delay and no unpaid amount; the plan guarantees indemnity at the value of the dwelling including every improvement. The one unexplained gap the card leaned on is not unexplained: the review states the project "resettled 83 families (three more than estimated at the time of additional financing)", which accounts for the difference from the plan's census of 80 (59 at Reta de Honório, 7 at Pilares, 14 at Deodoro). Plan-reprint check run across both numbers: the plan's 80 carries only future verbs ("será requerida a disponibilização de 80 soluções", "o processo de reassentamento das 80 famílias deverá acontecer"), and 83 appears in no plan, so the outcome figure is not a reprint — the row is a drop on the absence of loss, not on the figure. Parent link verified and the brief's "no reachable completion report" was wrong: the completion report at cache/P111996/ICR_2023-06-27_34110687.txt names "the Additional Finance approved on January 26, 2012 (P125630)" in its own text, its cover reads "LOANS 7719-BR AND 8117-BR ... UPGRADING AND GREENING THE RIO DE JANEIRO URBAN RAIL SYSTEM ( P111996 )", and the September 2011 plan is filed under both numbers.

The harm is a gap in paperwork, not a documented loss to anyone. The completion report of 30 April 2021, paragraph 97, is the whole of it: the social safeguard rating was downgraded at closing "because of pending issues related to the documentation of the payment of easement fees for 20 landholders affected by the works of the Pirangi-Camevô water main and the Surubim sanitation system", and the post-closing action plan requires "the provision of the evidence of payment of these easement fees". Documentation of payment is not non-payment, and no document found says any of the twenty went unpaid or was paid below replacement cost. Checked in the outcome documents: paragraph 98 of the same report records that the project "followed good practices related with social risk management, ensuring compliance with the requirements of OP 4.12 and OP 4.11"; paragraph 99, the only other resettlement sentence, says "at project closing, the compensation payment processes related to the project's infrastructure (right of way) were still pending judgment, and there were a few gaps in documenting the processes and the related evidence", and attaches no number, no site and no person to it; the evaluation review ICRR0022614 repeats paragraph 97 verbatim and adds nothing. The report's own Annex 6, the status annex for the post-closing plan, carries only environmental items — dam corrective works, erosion prevention, slope stabilisation, greenbelt planting, effluent reuse — and no social item, so the report does not carry the status of the thing its body says the plan contains. Land taken for right of way with no recorded loss is the shape this same batch drops at cordoba-road-right-of-way-land-donations. The only count of people resettled anywhere in the file is the appraisal document's statement that the Pirapama conveyance works, built with the state's counterpart money before the loan was approved, "have affected 294 families, including the resettlement of 202 families" — an appraisal figure for works the loan did not finance, with no outcome figure for it in any document. This is the closest call in the batch: if the owner reads paragraph 99's "pending judgment" as compensation unsettled at closing rather than as process paperwork, the row returns as limb (b), and the sentence is quoted here in full for that purpose.

No document records anyone relocated. The completion report for the Recife Urban Development and Social Inclusion Project (ICR3043, 14 April 2014) says at paragraph 44 that "at the time of Loan Closing the resettlement of about 760 families affected by the construction of the road system and bridge over the Capibaribe River, and integrated urban upgrading and macro-drainage works was still pending", and at paragraph 45 that the Bank "will continue supervising the resettlement of these 763 families" because the works will not be finished until June 2018. That is a count of families affected and awaiting a move, which the forward rule treats as a drop. Checked in the outcome documents: Table 2 of the same report, "Pending Works after Project Closing", lists the resettlement of 403 families for the Casarao do Barbalho housing complex and "at most 360 families" for the road and bridge as future events, both financed by national programmes (PAC and Minha Casa Minha Vida) rather than by the loan, and records that the borrower was revising the bridge designs to reduce the number of affected people and to spare a school. PDO indicator 5, resettled ZEIS households with legal land tenure, is reported as "Loan closed before relevant project components were completed. (TARGET NOT MET)" against a target of 100 per cent. The Independent Evaluation Group's review (ICRR14352) repeats the same 760 figure as a risk that "remains", adds nothing, and records no resettlement carried out. The only completed social output in the report is 581 people trained at a rehabilitated job centre. The appraisal document's 1,453 families to be resettled is a plan figure; the resettlement framework of 1 December 2005 says the plan establishing how many families are to be relocated would be executed in the project's first year, and no such count appears in an outcome document. Nothing in either outcome document records compensation unpaid, land taken, a death, an injury, an arrest or a livelihood lost.

Ten families, 57 people, were moved, but no document records a loss on top of the move, and the destination is better than the origin on the face of the documents. The completion report (30 December 2018) says at paragraph 65 that "a total of 10 families (57 people) were resettled from living within the wetlands recharge areas and a resettlement plan was reviewed by Bank social development specialists and implemented at the beginning of the project implementation", that the move freed wetland that recharges the island's aquifer, and that "no other resettlement or indigenous peoples' issues occurred during implementation". Checked in the outcome documents: the report's output list records "wetland recharge areas in Corn Islands recovered from human establishments" as achieved, and the Independent Evaluation Group's review (28 February 2019) says the project complied with all social and environmental safeguards and describes the plan without reporting any grievance or shortfall. The resettlement plan itself (Proyecto de Reasentamiento Poblacional Humedal Coe, Barrio Brig Bay No. 1, May 2012) is explicit on what the families got: the ten houses they were leaving were valued at an average of 25,000 córdobas each and the new houses at 178,000 córdobas each, "el costo de las nuevas viviendas superan en 600% al precio de avalúo de las viviendas del humedal"; they held neither title nor land in the wetland and were to be given title to the new plot by the municipality; the municipality was to move their belongings; and "hasta el momento, ninguna persona de las 10 familias ha mostrado resistencia u objeción al reasentamiento". The plan also records that in the wetland they were exposed to flooding and respiratory illness. ICIJ's estimate of 57 for this project is the same 57 people. Under the round 19 limit on limb (a) a relocation out of a hazard zone with secure tenure at the destination and no recorded loss is not a case.

The resettlement never happened. The appraisal document of 12 August 2004 said "The project has identified 60 families in Machu Picchu Pueblo that reside outside town boundaries on land extremely vulnerable to landslides. These families will be resettled within the pueblo or at an acceptable location identified outside the town", with a resettlement action plan in Annex 17 and a separate plan filed for 60 urban families. Checked in the outcome documents: the completion report of 19 December 2011 says "No resettlement in Machu Picchu Pueblo was to be carried out as analysis of risk financed with a GFDRR grant suggested the entire town was at risk, not just the 60 families originally identified", that the activity was changed to an early warning system and other risk management measures, and at paragraph 38 that "the resettlement safeguard was triggered originally but then detriggered during Project restructuring". Paragraph 51 repeats that "although the original aim was to relocate 60 households, this was dropped". The Independent Evaluation Group's review confirms that the resettlement policy was no longer triggered and that the housing construction activity was re-oriented to the early warning design. The only harm language in the documents is in the appraisal document's description of conditions before the project: falling stones that had struck the train, injuring three tourists, one of whom died of a heart attack, and the loss of life and property in Machu Picchu Pueblo in the floods that preceded the project. Those predate the project and were not caused by it. The outcome documents record no compensation unpaid, no land taken, no death, no injury and no arrest; the one social conflict they report is local opposition to any solution that would move the train station, which was not built.

Families were moved, but every document records the destination as better than the origin and no loss on top of the move. The completion report of 31 May 2023 says at paragraph 101 and in its results narrative that "105 families from the low-income, flood-prone urban area of El Porvenir in the Mosquera municipality were successfully resettled to a new neighborhood with improved living conditions, and 19 families opted for individual resettlement". Checked in the outcome documents: paragraph 103 gives the detail. El Porvenir was 124 buildings; the site of the move was agreed with the settlers in a consultation lasting more than two years; it was close enough to keep support networks, schooling and access to health and transport; "since the settlers did not own the land but did own the improvements, the resettlement implied that they now owned the land and the houses built"; a warehouse was built for the residents who make a living from recycling, 25 homes with 51 people; a park, green areas and a nursery were built beside the new settlement; a visit three years later found the houses well kept and extended; and "no complaints were filed during and after the resettlement process". On the river works, paragraph 102 says the purchase of about 320 strips of land along the river "did not imply transfer of people or limitations on existing activities; nor did it imply crop elimination" and that "the entire process was voluntary and did not require coercive actions, let alone the use of force". The Inspection Panel complaint of 2016 concerned the design of the El Salitre wastewater plant, not the resettlement: paragraph 92 records that the Panel did not recommend an investigation, and the Panel's nine recommendations, which led to a design change preserving a wetland, had all been met by 2020. The 188 households in the component description at page 12 are not a competing count of the El Porvenir families: that sentence describes Component 2, the river works, while the 105 and the 19 are reported under Component 3, and paragraph 102 says of the Component 2 land purchases that they "did not imply transfer of people or limitations on existing activities". There is no conflict between the two figures. Searches of Colombian sources in Spanish for the El Porvenir resettlement in Mosquera returned only World Bank blog posts. This is the same shape as the Bogotá Disaster Vulnerability Reduction case that round 19 dropped.

Land was taken for right of way, but no document records a loss to anyone, and both outcome documents record the transfers as voluntary donations with compensation in kind. The completion report of 21 April 2014 says at section 2.4.3 that "a total of 102 properties were affected by RoW acquisition. The loss of land suffered by the landowners was minor. In all cases, the land taken represents less than 7% of the total area of the property affected. The affected properties were large (between 500 and 10,000 hectares)", that landowners received compensation in kind such as new fencing and improved entrances, that "RoW acquisition did not cause physical displacement (relocation)", and that the landowners who donated land chose to do so and could have asked for expropriation instead: one did, and was compensated under an amicable agreement, the avenimiento. The report's footnote 17 says the Bank's resettlement policy "does not apply to the land donations that took place in the context of this project, given their voluntary nature" and applies only to that single expropriation. Checked in the outcome documents: the Independent Evaluation Group's review repeats those figures and adds that "the project relied to a considerable extent (the precise percentage is unknown) on voluntary donations of land", without finding a shortfall; it records no grievance, no unpaid compensation and no displacement. The one relocation the project might have caused, of informal vendors beside a new bridge over the Río Los Reartes, was avoided by changing the bridge's design and location. The harm language the pre-extraction surfaced for this row is road-safety material: the appraisal document's national road fatality rates and the completion report's claim of a fall in accidents and deaths after the road safety plan. Neither is harm by the project.

The land acquisition is counted in structures, not people, and no document records a loss to anyone; and the Bank did not finance the works that took the land. The completion report of 22 June 2021 says at paragraph 77 that the project "triggered OP 4.12 Involuntary Resettlement requiring land acquisition affecting 355 buildings (239 housing units and 116 commercial units)", that a resettlement action plan was prepared, not objected to by the Bank and "fully implemented until completion in 2015", that most affected people received cash compensation, and that 48 vulnerable families could choose between cash, a housing voucher and a new unit in a complex built by the state housing company. Owners of commercial premises were compensated in cash and told they could claim for foregone profits. In 2015 the metro company surveyed 176 affected people about their new homes, their takings and their neighbourhoods, and it ran a grievance mechanism through which more than 3,000 communications were received and redressed. The only adverse note is paragraph 67: "Resettlement for the civil works of Line 5 had a few emblematic cases in which residents or businesses resisted relocation in spite of the mutually beneficial solutions that were offered", with no count and no loss attached. A structure count cannot carry the displacement field, which on this map holds people, households or families. Checked in the outcome documents: the Independent Evaluation Group's review repeats the 355 buildings and the compensation options and records no shortfall; its statement that the project complied with the resettlement policy is attributed to a project team email of 17 August 2021, not to a document. Separately, the works that took the land were not financed by this credit: paragraph 60(a) of the completion report says "the World Bank-financed components of Line 5 are the acquisition of trains and the installation of CBTC systems and platform doors", and the appraisal document of 3 March 2010 says the civil works "will be financed and executed by the Borrower" and that construction accident risk "is an indirect risk because Bank is not involved in the civil works". The seven deaths at the Pinheiros station collapse of January 2007, which the Line 5 appraisal document describes, belong to Line 4 and are carried as a separate case.

Cut at check. The whole harm is footnote 23 of the completion report of 21 December 2016, which reads: 'In one of the khals eviction took place of an unknown number of people. A tracer study was expedited by DWASA. However due to the risk that these studies are incomplete, this khal was dropped. A total of seven khals were dropped due to complex resettlement issues.' Two things in that footnote decide it. First, the people are not identifiable in any sense the forward rule allows: no count, no canal, no date, and no account of what became of them, which is thinner than the standing edge case of five identified resettlement cases at a named site. Second, the footnote's own next clause is that the khal was dropped from the project, so no document ties the eviction to works the credit paid for; the footnote does not say who evicted anyone or why. The main text at paragraph 32 says no private land was acquired, that the two pumping stations affected 221 households and the canal works 216 households, and that these were adequately compensated; the review of 8 March 2017 does not mention the eviction at all. The point the card carried was Khilgaon, which is where a different incident happened, a partial building demolition on the Khilgaon-Bashabo canal right of way that the same paragraph records as adequately resolved, so the card would also have plotted the wrong canal. Two figures inside this one report disagree and are recorded in the check log rather than on a card: the main text and Annex 2 give 216 households compensated along the khals, while the borrower's section at page 43 says the improvements on the nine canals as a whole affected 187 persons or households, of which 67 were encroachers whose impacts it calls negligible and who the framework made ineligible for resettlement assistance.

Neither limb of the forward rule is met. The completion report of 30 January 2012 says of the whole project that POWERGRID ensures that its projects do not result in physical displacement of the local population, and that under this project social assessment and a rehabilitation action plan were done for the Wardha substation only. Its Annex 3 scheme table records the outcome for Wardha: the plan involved 89.20 acres of Maharashtra Industrial Development Corporation land, no land compensation was required to be paid to any project affected families as the land belonged to that corporation, and the plan was completed in March 2008 with rehabilitation assistance of INR 3.62 lakh distributed to all affected families and vocational training given to them at Krishi Kendra, Wardha. The three adverse findings checked all resolve: the report records that implementation of the plan was delayed by the long process of acquiring land and extending resettlement entitlements through the district administration, and that implementation of the community development part was unduly delayed by staffing constraints, which together with forest clearance delays got overall safeguard compliance downgraded to moderately satisfactory towards the end of 2008; the same paragraph records that an independent external agency's impact assessment found an improvement in the socioeconomic status of a majority of the affected people, and the rating was upgraded to satisfactory in early 2011. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 12 November 2012 gives the same account and adds nothing adverse. The only people-bearing figures in the project's resettlement papers are counts of people affected, not relocated, and they belong to another substation: the resettlement plan of 1 March 2007 covers the 400/220 kV Solapur substation at Limbi-Chincholi, giving 19 of 487 village households affected by the substation, 35 affected families and 129 people affected out of 2,278, and it is a plan for a scheme under Western Region System Strengthening II, not one of the four substations the completion report lists under this project. What is left is a count of people affected, which is a drop under the forward rule.

Neither limb of the forward rule is met. The completion report of 30 May 2020 records at paragraph 58 that the transmission lines and substations were built almost entirely in desert where the land belongs to the government and is mostly uninhabited; that a resettlement action plan was prepared only for the overhead line from the Gulf of Suez substation to the Samallout substation, because that line took land for tower footings and damaged crops temporarily around the inhabited areas at the Nile crossing; that the tower-footing land was acquired on a willing seller-willing buyer basis and crop damage was compensated at prevailing assessed market rates; that no significant disputes were recorded by the grievance mechanism, the cases received being mainly requests to explain how the compensation rates were worked out; and that no resettlement plans were prepared for the substations because all were on government-owned uninhabited desert land. The appraisal document of 19 May 2010 says no land acquisition is associated with almost 89 per cent of the route. The resettlement action plan of 1 February 2014 is a plan and gives 22 owners in its census; no outcome document carries that figure or any count of people moved. The occupational health and safety finding was checked: both the completion report and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 4 February 2021 record instances of non-compliance with occupational health and safety requirements and unsatisfactory on-site contractor performance, with the implementing utility hiring an independent consultancy late to monitor contractors, and both record that the efforts led to gradual improvement, insurance coverage for all workers and a workers' code of conduct. Neither document records a death, an injury, an arrest, land taken without payment or a livelihood not restored.

Neither limb of the forward rule is met. The completion report of 28 December 2015 says at paragraph 36 that although no land acquisition was envisaged at the inception of the project the involuntary resettlement policy was triggered to cover possible adverse impacts, and that overall implementation of social safeguards was rated satisfactory throughout the project period. The borrower's section lists the data gathered for the resettlement plan under the heading land required through voluntary donation. On outcomes, paragraph 38 says the great majority of the works were road widening, culverts and drainage, and that most adverse impacts observed during implementation were construction related: access to houses and shops, damage to houses and boundary walls, and damage to side drains and toilet structures. It attaches no count to any of these and records that grievance redress mechanisms were set up in all participating provinces with a robust review and monitoring system. The borrower's section says all project affected people identified were provided mitigation measures for their livelihoods. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 10 June 2016 adds nothing adverse on resettlement and repeats that implementation of social safeguards was deemed satisfactory throughout. No document counts anyone relocated, records compensation unpaid or below replacement cost, or records a death, injury, arrest or livelihood not restored.

Neither limb of the forward rule is met. The completion report of 19 December 2019 says at paragraph 58 that the project's environmental and social safeguards management was satisfactory, and lists the safeguards issues that arose: compensation for trees that were cut down, a dwelling that was obstructing the obstacle limitation survey, asbestos to be removed and disposed of at Bonriki, and a land claim associated with the Bonriki terminal. It then says all of these were resolved at the completion of the project, and gives no count, no outcome and no date for the dwelling. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 6 May 2020 repeats the same list and says all were successfully resolved by project completion. The land claim was checked in the project's own social safeguards report of 5 December 2013, which records an ongoing dispute between the government and owners over a strip of land underlying the airport terminal and car park, that the dispute went through the courts to the High Court and is now resolved, and in a footnote that the government has the option of compulsory acquisition but that the outcome to date is that the government will be paying the lease including arrears to landowners. That land was already under the terminal before the project. No document counts anyone relocated or records compensation unpaid at close, a death, an injury, an arrest or a livelihood not restored.

The outcome is land area plus a count of people affected, which round 22 settled is not limb (b). The completion report for this project is not in the harvest and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 12 September 2012 is the only route to it; the review cites it by paragraph. At its safeguards section the review reports, citing the completion report, that the government prepared a land acquisition and resettlement policy framework satisfactory to the Bank and that resettlement action plans were prepared for Hubli-Dharwar and Gulbarga; that the Gulbarga plan was later modified because the pipelines were re-directed onto unencumbered government land, which reduced the number of affected families; that the total land acquisition for the project involved 8.41 hectares affecting 215 families, primarily in the Hubli-Dharwar and Gulbarga areas; and, citing completion report paragraph 2.4.5, that the plans were satisfactorily implemented and there were no complaints. The review reports environmental and safeguard management rated satisfactory over the entire project, and records that the project team subsequently informed the Evaluation Group that the project complied with the environmental assessment policy, which is a staff statement and not a document. ICIJ's estimate for this project, 215, is to the person the review's count of families affected. No document counts anyone relocated or records compensation unpaid or below replacement cost, a death, an injury, an arrest or a livelihood not restored.

Neither limb of the forward rule is met. The completion report for this project is not in the harvest and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 22 May 2017 is the only route to it; the review cites it by page. The review reports full compliance with both the environmental assessment and involuntary resettlement policies, with safeguards instruments developed and disclosed before approval and a technical operations unit reporting quarterly on them. On the people whose living the project changed, it reports, citing the completion report, that all former waste pickers at the Yatta open dumpsite were given jobs, helped to find new jobs at the Joint Services Council, or trained to become economically independent, that under-age pickers were allowed into vocational schools, and that environmental and living conditions improved around the previous open dumpsites, which used to suffer from waste burning. The results indicator for compensation, settlements, employment and income-generating schemes for affected people, waste pickers and herders records 100 per cent of households against a target of 80 per cent. Land for the new landfill was paid for by a US$2.0 million borrower contribution. No document counts anyone relocated or records compensation unpaid or below replacement cost, a death, an injury, an arrest or a livelihood not restored. One figure in the review, that the project closed 19 uncontrolled dumpsites against a target of 17, is an output and not a harm.

Cut by the checker. Limb (b) is not met: the harm is a pending claim of unstated content, with no count, no sum, no date and no statement of what any claimant lost, and the sentence that carries it also records the opposite. The deciding sentence is in the Independent Evaluation Group’s review ICRR0021847, safeguards section: “The ICR provides little detail on the status of compliance with individual safeguard policies. However, it indicates that at project closing, all triggered safeguards were rated Moderately Satisfactory, but there were several pending social and safeguard issues relating to dam safety, the arrangements to get rid of hazardous materials linked to the control of the black fly nuisance, and claims from Kimbanseke project-affected persons (PAPs). SNEL did confirm that the rehabilitation of the people affected by the construction of the second Inga-Kinshasa T-Line was completed, and there was agreement with stakeholders on how to close the process (the line would not be put into operation until the payment process was concluded).” Kimbanseke is a commune of Kinshasa of over a million people, not a site, so this is thinner than bukoba-airport-resettlement-arrears, which is the standing edge for limb (b) and names a site and a count of cases. The project’s own completion report is not reachable on any route tried and the review is the only account of it. Other outcome material checked and found not to carry the case: the appraisal document’s 270 and 129 households are what the project expected to affect; the April 2011 draft resettlement plan for the project (RP1135 v2, the PMEDE involuntary resettlement plan) records in the past tense that 229 families were censused at the affected sites, 211 of them in Kinshasa with the largest number in Kimbanseke commune, that the amounts were negotiated and agreements on them formalised, and that 43 resident owners, 137 non-resident owners and 49 tenants or rent-free occupants were counted, but every loss in it carries a future verb — 141 houses and 1,537 fruit trees “will” be destroyed, US$2,315,477 of compensation is “provided for”, and the plan’s execution is given as a nine-month programme still to run. Joining that 2011 census to the 2018 pending claims would be the checker’s inference: neither document refers to the other. The review’s own data sheet material is kept in the log, including that the borrower contribution of US$38.0 million ended up nil and that the review records a disagreement inside the completion report, whose data sheet rates outcome Moderately Satisfactory while its main text rates it Moderately Unsatisfactory. ICIJ gives 266 for this project.

Neither limb of the forward rule is met. Outcome document checked: the completion report of 20 November 2015 (ICR3428), paragraph 68, the whole social safeguards paragraph. It says the involuntary resettlement policy was triggered, that of 89 subprojects for upgrading and expanding the distribution network under Component 1, 22 were found to require Resettlement Action Plans 'covering about 200 persons', that 'the resettlement aspect was related mainly to the impact on street vendors and artisans along the routes where the underground lines were replaced', and that the plans 'were successfully completed through regular supervision by the Bank and the PCU'. Compliance was rated satisfactory from 2009 to March 2011 and moderately satisfactory thereafter, the downgrade being attributed to the electoral crisis and then to delays in selecting a consulting firm to prepare the plans and hiring an extra expert. There is no count of anyone relocated, no unpaid compensation, no injury, arrest or death. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 12 August 2016 repeats the 200 and adds only that 'the ICR did not report findings of any independent review of the environmental safeguards or the social safeguards'. The July 2012 resettlement plan for Component 1 counts people affected per subproject as plan figures, falling as routes were redrawn (39 instead of 82 at the Azito resettlement site in Yopougon, 3 instead of 9 at BK Vatican, 6 instead of 13 at Yopougon gare), and attributes the drop at Yopougon gare to pavement clearances carried out by the Ministry of Urban Sanitation under its 'opération ville propre', not by the project; at Abobodoumé and Attécoubé it records that works already done had caused no impact. ICIJ gives 701 for this project.

Neither limb of the forward rule is met. Outcome document checked: the completion report of 26 June 2013 (ICR2630), paragraph 37, the whole safeguards paragraph, plus the solid waste outcome section at paragraph 54 and the borrower performance section at paragraph 84. Paragraph 37 records the one failing: 'During implementation a case of non-compliance with OP 4.12 was recorded for sanitation works at locations along the Metsurado River where solid waste cleanup was to be done. Works were stopped and deferred until the RAP was prepared.' The works were halted before anyone was moved, and the same paragraph concludes 'it is considered that overall safeguard compliance was satisfactory'; paragraph 84 adds that 'funding for resettlement was made available in a timely manner'. The outcome section records the volume of waste removed, 19 public toilets rehabilitated and the Whein Town landfill financed to about 80 per cent of works, and gives no count of anyone relocated and no compensation shortfall. The project's own resettlement plan of July 2008 identifies 99 households in the area to be cleared of refuse 'who will be displaced', a figure in a draft plan that no outcome document picks up. No evaluation review was reachable for this project. Independent reporting on the Whein Town landfill (FrontPage Africa, 29 September 2026) records residents' accounts of foul-smelling water, mosquitoes, rodents and malaria, with no test results, no illness counts and no compensation, and attributes the 2011 landfill to the Emergency Monrovia Urban Sanitation project rather than to this credit, so it cannot be tied to this financing. ICIJ gives 431 for this project. Checked and added by the checker: paragraph 43 of the same report says “the solid waste activities were curtailed after they exceeded the intermediate outcome and have been continued under the Bank funded EMUS Project”, which is why no harm at the Whein Town landfill attaches to this credit. The Emergency Monrovia Urban Sanitation project (P115664) is the credit the press account points to and is a separate row.

Dropped because the whole of it would be a count of people affected plus a compensation delay whose stated consequence is delay to the project, which the forward rule excludes. Outcome documents checked: the completion report of 21 June 2021, paragraphs 48 to 61, and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 2 December 2021, its safeguards section. The completion report's paragraph 57 says 'Adamawa, Enugu, and Osun states experienced delays in implementing Resettlement Action Plans (RAPs, with 2,423 affected persons compensated for a total amount of Naira123,528,553) occasioned by late release of counterpart funds by State Governments' — that is, all 2,423 were paid. Paragraph 49 adds that Enugu's unit received no funds in 2014 and 'were not able to cover operating expenses and payment of compensation under the Resettlement Action Plans', with total outstanding counterpart funding of Naira 3,591,869,010 at the October 2016 mid-term review. The review states the consequence the completion report does not: the delayed compensation 'slowed down project implementation and was one of the reasons for the project closing date extension'. There is no count of anyone relocated, no unpaid balance and no recorded loss to any identifiable person. The grievance mechanism logged 123 complaints, all addressed. The only other safeguards finding, that shrines were encountered along priority roads in Enugu State in June 2016 and the matter solved by revising an abbreviated resettlement plan, exists in the review solely as what 'the project team subsequently informed IEG', with the revised plan noted as 'not archived in WB docs'. Two kidnappings of contractor staff in Osun and Niger states between February and April 2019 are recorded; they are harm to the contractor's employees by third parties, not harm caused by the project. The 2015, 2016 and 2019 resettlement plans and addenda in the cache are all plans. ICIJ gives 428 for this project.

Dropped because no outcome document exists for this operation on any route tried, and every document that does exist is forward-looking. Documents checked: the updated Compensation and Resettlement Plan for the Inga–Zambia Electrical Interconnection Reinforcement of June 2008 (RP770, volumes 1 and 2) and the January 2008 updated study. They are plans throughout. The plan says 'SNEL promises to compensate all eligible persons', estimates the whole compensation at USD 1,042,482, of which USD 463,345.00 for loss of farm crops, puts replacement housing at about USD 230 per square metre in 2008 against USD 100 in 2003, and counts individuals and households that 'could be affected' over a cultivated area of 172 ha. Of the people interviewed for the update, it says 'since they know they will be relocated within the village, none of them feel dispossessed', and that in 2008 they 'are still confident about the compensation process' — both future-tense. Not one figure has a relocation or a payment verb attached. Route that failed: the Bank's wds query by this project number returns no completion report and no assessment report, and a qterm title search on the project name returns none filed under this number; the sibling operation P097201, the APL-1b phase, has an evaluation review but it reviews that project's own completion report and says nothing about the Inga–Zambia interconnection resettlement, beyond a Bank review of financial management covering both. ICIJ gives 410 for this project.

Neither limb of the forward rule is met. Outcome documents checked: the completion report of 12 June 2014 (ICR2982), paragraphs 34 to 36, the whole environment and social safeguards section, and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 24 March 2015, its safeguards section. The completion report says the project was Category B 'as no major environmental impacts were identified', that a framework was prepared and updated, that a screening mechanism was used to categorise the small subprojects submitted by the 67 municipalities, that 'a few simplified resettlement plans were also produced' and all were approved by the Bank, and that 'appropriate mitigation measures were prepared and implemented'. For the large inter-communal investments it says resettlement plans were produced and the recommendations 'approved by the Bank, implemented and monitored as appropriate'. The review adds only the completion report's sentence that 'the project complied with Bank fiduciary and safeguards policies'. Neither document counts a single person affected, relocated or compensated, names a site where land was taken, or records any injury, arrest, death or unpaid payment. The 2005 document in the cache is the resettlement policy framework, not a site plan. ICIJ gives 325 for this project.

Neither limb of the forward rule is met, and the one document that reports an outcome rests largely on what Bank staff told the evaluators. Outcome document checked: the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 1 September 2017, its whole safeguards section; no completion report for this project was reachable in the harvest. On the environmental side the review says 'the Bank team informed IEG that the environmental safeguards were complied with'. On the social side it says 'the Bank team informed the IEG that the social safeguards were complied with', and then gives the only recorded failing: 'The supervision missions of November 2012 and January 2013 observed that the ARAP document omitted some Project Affected Persons (PAPs) on one of the roads. The ARAP document was revised after several months of delay. The revised document was disclosed as an addendum to the ARAP. The process did not affect the progress of the works. The PAPs were compensated.' So the people left out were paid, the works were not held up, and no count, no unpaid sum and no loss to anyone is recorded; a resettlement implementation committee and a grievance committee were set up afterwards. The two resettlement documents in the cache, of March 2007 and November 2011, are a policy framework and an abbreviated plan. ICIJ gives 195 for this project. Checked and added by the checker: the clause after the staff statement on the environmental side reads “An independent audit did not reveal issues or concerns on compliance with safeguard policies”, so the review does not rest on the staff statement alone. The review carries no date on its cover or in its text; its report number is ICRR0020754 and the date of 1 September 2017 is the Bank document library’s own date for it, not the document’s.

already_on_map.note: ICIJ row P090374, VN-GEF-Coastal Cities Project, is the Global Environment Facility grant to the Coastal Cities Environmental Sanitation Project and is already on the map as quy-nhon-coastal-cities-sanitation-resettlement, which already carries the GEF grant TF094335 in its lender list. The documents harvested for this row are the same joint completion report of 2015 the existing case cites, covering P082295, P122940 and P090374, plus the appraisal document for the GEF grant and three Quy Nhon resettlement plans. Nothing in them adds a fact the existing case does not already carry: its 189.4 hectares, 1,247 affected households, 223 resettled against 245 planned, 259 land plots on five sites, VND 233 billion paid, and VND 3 billion placed in treasury accounts for 11 Quy Nhon households, are all in paragraphs 49 to 51 of that report. No extend is offered. One correction is reported rather than written into the file because fields_add cannot change a number: the existing case carries displaced: 1247, which is the completion report's count of affected households, while the report's count of households resettled is 223. Checker's addition to that correction: both figures are three-city totals. The completion report's sentence is "The project acquired around 189.4 ha of land in all three cities, with 1,247 affected HHs, of which 223 HHs had to be resettled", covering Quy Nhon, Nha Trang and Dong Hoi, and the report gives no Quy Nhon-only breakdown of either number. So 223 should not simply replace 1,247 on a card named for Quy Nhon; whichever number is carried, the label has to say it is the three-city total.

Fostering Agricultural Productivity Project (P095091), Mali, is already on the map as mali-office-du-niger-hamlets, confirmed by place (Sabalibougou perimeter, Office du Niger) and by years. The documents harvested for this row are the completion report of 14 February 2020, which the existing case already uses, and the Independent Evaluation Group review of 22 May 2020 (filed under the title 'Mali - Mali-Agricultural Productivity GEF (SIP)'). The review adds no fact the existing case does not carry: it repeats that a resettlement action plan was prepared to displace four hamlets, that some households received 3 hectares rather than the 5 the plan stated, and that an environmental and social specialist was never hired, safeguards being handled by consultants hired by the Office du Niger. Being a review of the same completion report, it would not move the case from contested to documented either. No extend is proposed.
